_meta.elementTitle: Plan and prepare to work at heights

element.title: Plan and prepare to work at heights
performanceCriteria: 1.1 Work requirements, including scope and nature of work are determined from work plans and specifications in accordance with workplace procedures
1.2 Potential hazards are identified and risk control measures are selected in consultation with the work team and supervisor
1.3 Equipment and materials are selected and checked for serviceability and compliance with workplace procedures and statutory requirements
1.4 Access and egress routes to and from the work area are confirmed to minimise risk

workplaceDocuments.title: SWMS-HAW-001: Working at Heights Safe Work Method Statement
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Step 1: Complete pre-start inspection of all equipment. Step 2: Verify exclusion zone established below work area. Step 3: Confirm rescue plan with supervisor before ascending.

workplaceDocuments.title: SOP-EQ-042: Scaffold Inspection Procedure
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Daily inspection required before use. Check: base plates level, bracing secure, platforms complete, guardrails at 900-1100mm, toe boards in place.

workplaceDocuments.title: JHA-ROOF-015: Roof Access Job Hazard Analysis
workplaceDocuments.keyContent: Hazards: Falls from height, fragile surfaces, weather conditions. Controls: Edge protection, safety mesh, harness attachment points every 2m along roof line.

cards.title: Reading Work Plans Before You Climb
cards.description: Before starting any work at heights, you must understand exactly what the job involves. Work plans tell you what needs to be done, where, and how to do it safely.
requirements: Locate the SWMS for your specific task before accessing the work area
Identify the exact work location, height, and duration from the work plan
Confirm the scope includes all tasks you'll perform at height
Check that the work plan matches current site conditions
Verify the plan is current and approved as per site procedures
doList: Read the complete SWMS before starting work
Ask your supervisor if any details are unclear
Check the plan covers your specific trade tasks
dontList: Assume yesterday's plan still applies today
Skip reading because you've done similar work before
Start work if the plan doesn't match site conditions

documentReference.title: SWMS-HAW-001
documentReference.relevantSection: Step 1: Complete pre-start inspection of all equipment

cards.title: The Missing Scope
cards.situation: You're a carpenter assigned to install roof battens on a new house. Your supervisor hands you a SWMS for 'general roofing work' but it doesn't mention batten installation. The other crew members are already on the roof.
cards.complication: The foreman says 'Just get up there, the SWMS covers roofing.' You notice the SWMS was created for tile laying, not carpentry work, and doesn't include the power tools you'll be using.
cards.decisionPoint: What should you do before climbing onto the roof?

mentalModel.application: The PLAN must match the DO - if your work isn't in the plan, the controls might not protect you

cards.voiceoverText: Picture this: You're a carpenter on a house build. The foreman hands you a roofing SWMS, but it's actually for tile laying - your batten work isn't mentioned. The crew's already up there, waiting. Do you follow them up, or stop and question the plan?

cards.question: Based on the scenario, what is the BEST course of action before starting work?

options.text: Proceed to the roof since the SWMS covers 'general roofing work' and you're experienced
options.feedback: Experience doesn't replace proper documentation. The SWMS must specifically cover your tasks and equipment.

options.text: Request the supervisor update the SWMS to include batten installation and your power tools before you start
options.feedback: Correct. PC 1.1 requires work requirements match the work plan. An incomplete SWMS means incomplete risk controls.

options.text: Complete the work quickly then ask for the SWMS to be updated afterwards
options.feedback: Working without proper controls exposes you to uncontrolled risks. Updates must happen before work begins.

options.text: Sign the SWMS anyway since the foreman approved it
options.feedback: Your signature confirms the controls are adequate for YOUR work. You share legal responsibility.

cards.correctExplanation: Requesting an updated SWMS ensures all hazards from your specific work are identified and controlled. Under WHS law, you have the right - and responsibility - to ensure the SWMS covers your actual tasks.
cards.incorrectConsequence: Working under an inadequate SWMS means power tool hazards, fall distances, and rescue procedures for carpentry work haven't been assessed. If an incident occurs, investigators will find the SWMS didn't match the work performed.
cards.keyTakeaway: Your SWMS must match your work scope exactly. Never sign off on a plan that doesn't cover what you're actually doing.
cards.documentGrounding: SWMS-HAW-001 requires task-specific risk assessment before work commences

checklistItems.text: I have read the SWMS for my specific task
The work plan matches my actual work scope
I understand the height, location, and duration of work
The plan was approved and is current for today's conditions

terminology.definition: The specific tasks, equipment, and methods that define what work will be performed. Must be documented in the SWMS before work begins.

reflection.question: Think about a time you saw work being done that wasn't covered by the plan. What risks were uncontrolled?

cards.title: Finding Hazards Before They Find You
cards.description: Every height work task has hazards that can cause serious injury or death. Your job is to identify them with your team before anyone climbs up.
requirements: Walk the work area at ground level to identify overhead and underfoot hazards
Consult with your work team about hazards they've experienced on similar tasks
Check the JHA for known hazards specific to this work location
Consider changing conditions: weather, nearby work, public access
Discuss control options with your supervisor before finalising the approach
doList: Complete a team toolbox talk identifying hazards for this specific job
Use the JHA as a starting point, not the final answer
Speak up if you notice something that wasn't in the risk assessment
dontList: Rely only on your own experience - the team sees more together
Assume hazards are the same as yesterday
Stay quiet if you're uncomfortable with the controls selected

documentReference.title: JHA-ROOF-015
documentReference.relevantSection: Hazards: Falls from height, fragile surfaces, weather conditions

cards.title: The New Hazard
cards.situation: Your team is setting up to replace guttering on a two-storey building. You completed the JHA last week and everyone signed off. This morning, you notice the building next door has started demolition work - there's dust, noise, and occasional debris falling near your work area.
cards.complication: The supervisor says the JHA was done properly and there's pressure to start because the client is waiting. One of your crew suggests 'just keeping an eye on the demo work' as a control.
cards.decisionPoint: The demolition work wasn't in your original JHA. What should happen next?

mentalModel.application: Site conditions change daily. Your risk controls must change with them.

cards.voiceoverText: Your guttering job seemed straightforward last week when you did the JHA. But today, there's a demolition crew next door throwing debris around. The original plan didn't account for this. The client's waiting, your crew's ready - but the conditions have changed.

cards.question: What is the BEST response to the changed site conditions?

options.text: Proceed with extra caution since the JHA was properly completed last week
options.feedback: A JHA captures hazards at a point in time. New hazards require new controls.

options.text: Stop work, update the JHA to include demolition hazards, and agree new controls with the team and supervisor
options.feedback: Correct. PC 1.2 requires hazard identification in consultation with the team. New hazards = new consultation.

options.text: Move to the opposite side of the building away from the demolition
options.feedback: This might help, but without documenting the hazard and controls, you're working outside your risk assessment.

options.text: Ask the demolition crew to stop while you complete your work
options.feedback: You can't control another contractor's work. Your controls must manage the hazard on your side.

cards.correctExplanation: Stopping to update the JHA isn't being difficult - it's being professional. Demolition creates airborne debris, noise distraction, and potential structural vibration. All of these affect your height work. The team consultation ensures everyone knows the new risks.
cards.incorrectConsequence: Working with unassessed hazards means your existing controls (harnesses, edge protection) might not be enough. A piece of demolition debris striking a worker on a ladder isn't covered by fall prevention equipment.
cards.keyTakeaway: When conditions change, your risk assessment must change. Stop, consult, update, then work.
cards.documentGrounding: JHA-ROOF-015 explicitly requires consideration of 'nearby work' as a hazard category

checklistItems.text: I have identified hazards with my work team
We have consulted with the supervisor on control measures
Controls are selected based on the hierarchy of control

terminology.definition: The ranked order of control effectiveness: Elimination, Substitution, Isolation, Engineering, Administration, PPE. Always start at the top.

reflection.question: When was the last time you stopped work because conditions changed? What happened?

cards.title: Checking Equipment That Keeps You Alive
cards.description: Height safety equipment is the last line of defence between you and a fall. Every piece must be inspected before use - your life depends on it.
requirements: Select equipment rated for the task: load capacity, fall distance, anchor strength
Complete a visual inspection of harnesses, lanyards, and connectors before each use
Check for current inspection tags on scaffolds and elevated work platforms
Verify all equipment meets Australian Standards as marked on labels
Report and remove defective equipment from service immediately
doList: Use the SOP-EQ-042 checklist for systematic equipment inspection
Check webbing for cuts, abrasion, chemical damage, or UV degradation
Confirm all carabiners and hooks lock properly and gates spring closed
dontList: Use equipment without an inspection tag or with an expired tag
Assume equipment is fine because it was used yesterday
Put defective equipment back in storage 'for someone else to check'

documentReference.title: SOP-EQ-042
documentReference.relevantSection: Daily inspection required before use. Check: base plates level, bracing secure, platforms complete, guardrails at 900-1100mm, toe boards in place

cards.title: The Frayed Lanyard
cards.situation: You're about to start work on a scaffold at 8 metres. During your pre-start harness check, you notice the webbing on your lanyard has some minor fraying near the stitching. The damage is small - about 10mm of surface wear.
cards.complication: The only spare lanyard on site is a different type that connects differently to your harness. Your supervisor is in a meeting and the job has a deadline. Your workmate says 'That tiny bit of wear won't matter for one day.'
cards.decisionPoint: The frayed lanyard is the equipment you've been issued. What should you do?

mentalModel.application: Height safety equipment has zero tolerance for damage - any defect could mean complete failure under load

cards.voiceoverText: You've got a job to do at 8 metres. Your harness checks out, but the lanyard has fraying near the stitching. Your mate says it's fine for one day, the spare doesn't fit properly, and the supervisor's unavailable. But that lanyard is what catches you if you fall.

cards.question: What is the correct response to the damaged lanyard?

options.text: Use the frayed lanyard carefully since the damage is minor and only for today
options.feedback: Any visible damage to fall arrest equipment requires immediate removal from service. 'Minor' damage can cause complete failure.

options.text: Tag the lanyard as defective, wait for supervisor guidance on the alternate equipment or replacement
options.feedback: Correct. PC 1.3 requires equipment be checked for serviceability. Defective equipment must be removed and reported before alternative arrangements are made.

options.text: Use the different lanyard type even though the connection is unfamiliar
options.feedback: Using unfamiliar equipment without training creates its own hazard. Proper equipment matching and competency is required.

options.text: Work without the lanyard since the scaffold has guardrails
options.feedback: Guardrails and harnesses serve different purposes. Your SWMS likely requires both for this height.

cards.correctExplanation: Tagging and removing the lanyard protects you and every future user. Waiting for supervisor guidance ensures you get compatible equipment and proper instruction. The delay is far less costly than a fall.
cards.incorrectConsequence: Frayed webbing has reduced strength. Fall arrest forces can be extreme — damaged fibres may fail instantly under load. The 'minor' wear you dismissed could be the difference between an arrested fall and a fatality.
cards.keyTakeaway: If equipment shows ANY damage, tag it out. Never use compromised height safety gear - there's no 'safe enough' level of damage.
cards.documentGrounding: SOP-EQ-042 requires removal of damaged equipment from service and immediate reporting

checklistItems.text: Equipment is rated for my task (load, height, anchor)
I have completed visual inspection before use
All tags and Australian Standards markings are present and current
Defective equipment has been tagged out and reported

terminology.definition: Equipment is in proper working condition with no damage, wear, or defects that could affect its performance. Verified through systematic inspection.

reflection.question: Have you ever felt pressure to use equipment you weren't sure about? How did you handle it?

cards.title: Planning Your Way Up and Down
cards.description: How you get to your work position matters as much as the work itself. Safe access and emergency egress routes must be confirmed before you start.
requirements: Identify the primary access route to the work area and confirm it's clear
Locate the emergency egress route and verify it remains accessible
Confirm ladder angles meet the 4:1 ratio (1 out for every 4 up)
Ensure scaffold access stairs or ladders have handrails and are unobstructed
Verify the rescue plan access points align with the routes you'll use
doList: Walk the access route before climbing to check for obstructions
Keep three points of contact when using ladders or access stairs
Maintain access routes clear of tools, materials, and debris during work
dontList: Climb external scaffold frames instead of using internal access ladders
Block the egress route with materials or equipment
Assume someone else has checked the access route

documentReference.title: SWMS-HAW-001
documentReference.relevantSection: Step 3: Confirm rescue plan with supervisor before ascending

cards.title: The Blocked Ladder
cards.situation: You're ready to access a scaffold for afternoon work. The internal access ladder on Level 2 has been blocked by another trade storing plasterboard sheets across the landing. They've gone to lunch and won't be back for 30 minutes.
cards.complication: Your work is time-critical and your supervisor said to get started. The external scaffold bracing looks climbable, and you've seen others use it as a shortcut. The proper access is blocked but you could work around it.
cards.decisionPoint: The formal access route is obstructed. What is the safe approach?

mentalModel.application: Your access route is also your emergency egress. If you can't get down safely, you can't get up safely.

cards.voiceoverText: The scaffold ladder is blocked by plasterboard from another trade. They're at lunch. You could climb the external bracing like others do, or wait 30 minutes for the route to clear. The job's time-critical, but the access you planned to use isn't available.

cards.question: What should you do when the formal access route is blocked?

options.text: Climb the external scaffold bracing since others do it and it's only temporary
options.feedback: External bracing is not designed for climbing. It lacks handholds, is not load-rated for climbing, and often has pinch points.

options.text: Wait until the obstruction is cleared or find an alternative formal access route before ascending
options.feedback: Correct. PC 1.4 requires confirmed access routes. Obstructed routes must be cleared or alternatives identified before work begins.

options.text: Move the plasterboard yourself to clear the access
options.feedback: Moving another trade's materials creates liability issues and potential manual handling hazards if done incorrectly.

options.text: Start work on Level 1 instead and do Level 2 later
options.feedback: This changes your work plan without consultation. Your SWMS may specify a work sequence for safety reasons.

cards.correctExplanation: Waiting or finding an alternative formal route ensures your access doubles as emergency egress. If an incident occurred and the route was blocked, rescue would be delayed. The 30-minute wait is a small investment in your safety.
cards.incorrectConsequence: Workers who climb scaffold bracing risk falls from unexpected failure, hand injuries from pinch points, and disciplinary action for unsafe work practices. More critically, if you're injured at height with the access blocked, rescuers face the same obstruction.
cards.keyTakeaway: Never improvise access. If your planned route is blocked, solve the problem before you climb - your egress depends on it.
cards.documentGrounding: SWMS-HAW-001 requires confirmed rescue plan access points before ascending

checklistItems.text: Primary access route is clear and confirmed
Emergency egress route is identified and accessible
Ladder angle meets 4:1 ratio if ladder access used
Rescue plan access points align with my routes

terminology.definition: The route used to exit a work area, especially during emergencies. Must remain clear and accessible at all times during work at heights.

reflection.question: Could you evacuate your current work area within 2 minutes if needed? What would slow you down?

format.detail: All 4 topics have exactly 5 cards each

mcqSingleAnswer.detail: All decision cards have exactly 1 correct option

antiRepetition.detail: No verb repetition >3x in knowledge requirements

documentGrounded.detail: No absolute claims without 'as per' qualifier

trainingValue.detail: Concrete consequences, not generic safety language
